title: Energy in Electromagnetic Waves
lead: An electromagnetic wave carries energy because its electric and magnetic fields exert forces on charges and move them, and the larger those fields are the more work they can do. This section shows that the energy a wave carries goes as the square of its amplitude, which for an electromagnetic wave is the maximum field strength, writes the average intensity of a sinusoidal wave three equivalent ways, notes that the intensity at the crest is twice the average, and works a microwave oven from the power it delivers and the area it delivers it over to both of its field strengths.
objectives: Explain how the energy and amplitude of an electromagnetic wave are related.
Given its power output and the heating area, calculate the intensity of a microwave oven’s electromagnetic field, as well as its peak electric and magnetic field strengths.
summary_html:
• The energy carried by any wave is proportional to its amplitude squared. For electromagnetic waves, this means intensity can be expressed as $$\kIave = \frac{\kc\varepsilon_0\kEfo^2}{2},$$ where $\kIave$ is the average intensity in $\text{W/m}^2$, and $\kEfo$ is the maximum electric field strength of a continuous sinusoidal wave.
  • This can also be expressed in terms of the maximum magnetic field strength $\kBmago$ as $$\kIave = \frac{\kc\kBmago^2}{2\mu_0}$$ and in terms of both electric and magnetic fields as $$\kIave = \frac{\kEfo\kBmago}{2\mu_0}.$$
  • The three expressions for $\kIave$ are all equivalent.

figures.original_caption: Energy carried by a wave is proportional to its amplitude squared. With electromagnetic waves, larger $E$-fields and $B$-fields exert larger forces and can do more work.

exercises.prompt: An old microwave oven outputs only half the electric field it used to. How much longer does it take to cook things in this microwave oven?

answer.hint: The energy a wave carries goes as the square of its field strength, so halving the field leaves a quarter of the intensity, and a quarter of the intensity delivers the same energy in four times the time.

exercises.prompt: Describe at least two improvements you could make to a radar set to make it more sensitive (able to detect things at longer ranges). Explain why these would work.

answer.solution: Raise the power the set transmits, and enlarge the antenna it receives with. The intensity of the wave that comes back falls off with the square of the distance to the target and back again, so at a longer range the returning wave is very weak, and the set can detect a target only while that returning wave is strong enough to drive its receiver. Putting out more power raises the intensity of the outgoing wave and of the echo in the same proportion, which means the echo from a more distant target is still large enough to read. A larger antenna helps for a different reason: the power the receiver collects is the intensity multiplied by the area the antenna presents to the wave, so doubling the area doubles the power gathered from an echo of a given intensity. Either change lets the set work with a fainter echo, and so at a longer range.

exercises.prompt: What is the intensity of an electromagnetic wave with a peak electric field strength of 125 V/m?

answer.hint: Put the peak electric field straight into $\kIave = \kc\varepsilon_0\kEfo^2/2$.

exercises.prompt: Assume the helium-neon lasers commonly used in student physics laboratories have power outputs of 0.250 mW. (a) If such a laser beam is projected onto a circular spot 1.00 mm in diameter, what is its intensity? (b) Find the peak magnetic field strength. (c) Find the peak electric field strength.

parts.hint: The spot is a circle 1.00 mm across, so its area is $\pi r^2$ with $r = 0.500$ mm.
The electric amplitude is the magnetic one multiplied by the speed of light.

exercises.prompt: Suppose the maximum safe intensity of microwaves for human exposure is taken to be $1.00\;\text{W/m}^2$. (a) If a radar unit leaks 10.0 W of microwaves (other than those sent by its antenna) uniformly in all directions, how far away must you be to be exposed to an intensity considered to be safe? Assume that the power spreads uniformly over the area of a sphere with no complications from absorption or reflection. (b) What is the maximum electric field strength at the safe intensity? (Note that early radar units leaked more than modern ones do. This caused identifiable health problems, such as cataracts, for people who worked near them.)

parts.hint: The leaked power spreads over a sphere, so the area is $4\pi r^2$; set the intensity there equal to the safe value and solve for $r$.
Rearrange $\kIave = \kc\varepsilon_0\kEfo^2/2$ for $\kEfo$ at the safe intensity.

exercises.prompt: Lasers can be constructed that produce an extremely high intensity electromagnetic wave for a brief time—called pulsed lasers. They are used to ignite nuclear fusion, for example. Such a laser may produce an electromagnetic wave with a maximum electric field strength of $1.00\times 10^{11}\;\text{V/m}$ for a time of 1.00 ns. (a) What is the maximum magnetic field strength in the wave? (b) What is the intensity of the beam? (c) What energy does it deliver on a $1.00\;\text{mm}^2$ area?

parts.hint: Divide the electric amplitude by the speed of light.
The energy is the intensity multiplied by the area and by the time the pulse lasts.

exercises.prompt: Suppose a source of electromagnetic waves radiates uniformly in all directions in empty space where there are no absorption or interference effects. (a) Show that the intensity is inversely proportional to $r^2$, the distance from the source squared. (b) Show that the magnitudes of the electric and magnetic fields are inversely proportional to $r$.
Integrated Concepts What capacitance is needed in series with an $800\;\mu\text{H}$ inductor to form a circuit that radiates a wavelength of 196 m?

answer.hint: The wavelength gives the frequency through $\kc = f\lambda$, and that frequency must be the resonant frequency $f_0 = 1/2\pi\sqrt{LC}$ of the circuit.

exercises.prompt: Integrated Concepts Assume the mostly infrared radiation from a heat lamp acts like a continuous wave with wavelength $1.50\;\mu\text{m}$. (a) If the lamp’s 200-W output is focused on a person’s shoulder, over a circular area 25.0 cm in diameter, what is the intensity in $\text{W/m}^2$? (b) What is the peak electric field strength? (c) Find the peak magnetic field strength. (d) How long will it take to increase the temperature of the 4.00-kg shoulder by $2.00^\circ\text{C}$, assuming no other heat transfer and given that its specific heat is $3.47\times 10^{3}\;\text{J/kg}\cdot{}^\circ\text{C}$?

parts.hint: The lit area is a circle 25.0 cm across, so it is $\pi r^2$ with $r = 12.5$ cm.
Divide the electric amplitude by the speed of light.
The heat needed is $mc\Delta T$, and the lamp delivers its 200 W to the shoulder the whole time.

exercises.prompt: Integrated Concepts Electromagnetic radiation from a 5.00-mW laser is concentrated on a $1.00\;\text{mm}^2$ area. (a) What is the intensity in $\text{W/m}^2$? (b) Suppose a 2.00-nC static charge is in the beam. What is the maximum electric force it experiences? (c) If the static charge moves at 400 m/s, what maximum magnetic force can it feel?

parts.hint: Find the peak electric field from the intensity, then use $F = qE_0$ with the peak field.
Find the peak magnetic field from the peak electric field, then use $F = qvB_0$ with the peak field.

exercises.prompt: Integrated Concepts If electric and magnetic field strengths vary sinusoidally in time, being zero at $t = 0$, then $\kEf = \kEfo\sin 2\pi ft$ and $\kBmag = \kBmago\sin 2\pi ft$. Let $f = 1.00\;\text{GHz}$ here. (a) When are the field strengths first zero? (b) When do they reach their most negative value? (c) How much time is needed for them to complete one cycle?

parts.part: (a) when the field strengths are first zero
parts.hint: Read the question as it is written: the fields are said to be zero at the start.
A sine is at its most negative three quarters of the way through a cycle.
One cycle takes the period, which is one divided by the frequency.

exercises.prompt: Unreasonable Results The peak magnetic field strength in a residential microwave oven is $9.20\times 10^{-5}\;\text{T}$. (a) What is the intensity of the microwave? (b) What is unreasonable about this result? (c) What is wrong about the premise?

answer.hint: Put the peak magnetic field into $\kIave = \kc\kBmago^2/2\mu_0$, then compare the answer with the few kilowatts per square metre a real oven delivers.
answer.solution:
(a) $1.01\times 10^{6}\;\text{W/m}^2$

(b) Much too great for an oven.

(c) The assumed magnetic field is unreasonably large.

exercises.prompt: Unreasonable Results An $\text{LC}$ circuit containing a 1.00-pF capacitor oscillates at such a frequency that it radiates at a 300-nm wavelength. (a) What is the inductance of the circuit? (b) What is unreasonable about this result? (c) Which assumptions are unreasonable or inconsistent?

answer.hint: The wavelength gives the frequency through $\kc = f\lambda$, and that frequency set equal to $1/2\pi\sqrt{LC}$ gives the inductance.
answer.solution:
(a) $2.53\times 10^{-20}\;\text{H}$

(b) $L$ is much too small.

(c) The wavelength is unreasonably small.

exercises.prompt: Critical Thinking (a) Find the magnetic field strength when the electric field strength is 1,250 V/m. (b) If E is increased, would B be increased, decreased, or remain the same? (c) By what factor would the change in part b be, if any?

answer.hint: In a vacuum the two field strengths of a wave stand in a fixed ratio, and that ratio is the speed of light.
answer.solution:
(a) $\kBmag = \frac{\kEf}{\kc} = \frac{1250}{3.00\times 10^{8}}\;\text{T} = 4.17\times 10^{-6}\;\text{T}$

(b) $B$ would increase.

(c) It would be by $1/\kc$.
